title: Thyroid eye disease and Graves' orbitopathy: recognising sight-threatening features

guidelineVersions: Bartalena L, Kahaly GJ, Baldeschi L, et al. The 2021 European Group on Graves' Orbitopathy (EUGOGO) clinical practice guidelines for the medical management of Graves' orbitopathy. European Journal of Endocrinology 2021;185(4):G43-G67

related.why: Thyroid anatomy and the nerves at risk in thyroid surgery
Thyroid nodule work-up, met in the same endocrine content area

brief.scenario: Claire Wetherby, 44, has Graves' disease. She reports new diplopia, gritty eyes and increasing prominence of both eyes.
brief.task: Recognise thyroid eye disease and identify features requiring urgent ophthalmology assessment.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Ask and examine for sight-threatening features first; thyroid control does not guarantee eye disease is settled.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Assuming normal or controlled thyroid function excludes thyroid eye disease, or waiting for thyroid results before referring urgent features.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd consider thyroid eye disease and specifically ask about visual acuity, colour vision, diplopia and pain."

flow: Recognise thyroid eye disease in the context of Graves' disease

grid.label: Recognising thyroid eye disease
grid.fail: Does not link the eye symptoms to Graves' disease, or dismisses the presentation as purely cosmetic.
grid.pass: Considers thyroid eye disease associated with Graves' disease given the diplopia, gritty eyes and proptosis.
grid.high: Adds that disease activity (inflammation, changing over weeks) and severity (structural and functional impact) are separate concepts that both need assessing.

grid.label: Targeted history
grid.fail: Takes a generic history without asking about visual acuity, diplopia, pain or colour vision.
grid.pass: Asks about visual acuity, colour vision, diplopia, pain, photophobia, ocular surface symptoms and change in appearance.
grid.high: Structures the questions specifically to screen for sight-threatening disease rather than general symptom review.

grid.label: Targeted examination
grid.fail: Only comments on the visible proptosis, without a structured eye examination.
grid.pass: Examines visual acuity, pupils, colour vision, eye movements, proptosis, eyelid position, conjunctival and corneal involvement and optic-nerve function.
grid.high: Explains how each finding maps to disease severity, for example an afferent pupillary defect suggesting optic nerve involvement.

grid.label: Urgent referral triggers
grid.fail: Would wait for thyroid function tests to normalise before considering ophthalmology referral, or cannot name a sight-threatening feature.
grid.pass: Arranges prompt ophthalmology assessment for visual deterioration, colour-vision change, an afferent pupillary defect, significant corneal exposure or other evidence of severe disease.
grid.high: Adds that these features suggest compressive optic neuropathy or severe corneal exposure specifically, which is why they are treated as urgent regardless of thyroid status.

grid.label: General measures
grid.fail: Offers no general measures, or tells the patient the eyes will return completely to normal once the thyroid is controlled.
grid.pass: Ensures thyroid function is appropriately managed and specifically advises smoking cessation.
grid.high: Adds that smoking is an important modifiable risk factor for both onset and severity of thyroid eye disease, and that significant disease needs specialist multidisciplinary care.

grid.label: Management is not one-size-fits-all
grid.fail: States that all thyroid eye disease should be treated with surgery.
grid.pass: States that management depends on activity and severity, with surgical treatment reserved for specific indications once disease activity has been assessed.
grid.high: Adds that decompression, strabismus and eyelid surgery each have a different role, timed by activity; sight-threatening disease needs urgent medical treatment first.

failures.move: Waiting for thyroid function to normalise before referring sight-threatening features.
failures.consequence: Compressive optic neuropathy or severe corneal exposure can progress while referral is delayed.

failures.move: Telling the patient the eyes will return completely to normal once the thyroid is controlled.
failures.consequence: This is inaccurate reassurance, since thyroid eye disease can occur or persist despite controlled thyroid function.

failures.move: Treating all thyroid eye disease with surgery.
failures.consequence: Surgery is applied without regard to disease activity, when it is timed and indicated according to activity and severity.

failures.move: Taking a generic history without asking about vision, colour vision, diplopia or pain.
failures.consequence: An early sight-threatening feature can be missed before examination even starts.

failures.move: Commenting only on the visible proptosis without a structured eye examination.
failures.consequence: Findings such as an afferent pupillary defect or corneal exposure are missed.

recovery.when: Asked whether normal thyroid function excludes the diagnosis
recovery.line: No. Thyroid eye disease can occur despite apparently controlled thyroid function.

recovery.when: Unsure which feature is most urgent
recovery.line: I'd prioritise anything suggesting optic nerve compromise or severe corneal exposure.

knowledge.fact: Thyroid eye disease can occur despite apparently controlled thyroid function; disease activity and severity are separate concepts.

Sight-threatening features are visual deterioration, colour-vision change, an afferent pupillary defect and significant corneal exposure, suggesting compressive optic neuropathy or severe corneal exposure.
Smoking cessation is specifically advised for all patients with Graves' hyperthyroidism, with or without eye disease.

recall.think: Compressive optic neuropathy or severe corneal exposure threatening sight.
recall.say: "I'd screen specifically for visual deterioration, colour-vision change, an afferent pupillary defect and corneal exposure."
do: Ask about acuity, colour vision, diplopia and pain
Examine acuity, pupils, movements, proptosis, cornea
Refer urgently if any sight-threatening feature present

recall.finish: Urgent ophthalmology assessment for sight-threatening features; smoking cessation; specialist multidisciplinary care for significant disease.

partner.opening: "Claire Wetherby, 44, has Graves' disease. She reports new diplopia, gritty eyes and increasing prominence of both eyes. Recognise thyroid eye disease and identify features requiring urgent ophthalmology assessment."

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about visual acuity and colour vision
reveals.finding: Visual acuity is mildly reduced on the right; colour vision (Ishihara) is subjectively desaturated on the right compared with the left.
A relative afferent pupillary defect is present on the right.

push.question: Does normal thyroid function exclude thyroid eye disease?
What makes the disease sight-threatening?
push.expect: Features suggesting optic nerve compromise or severe corneal exposure.

push.question: Is smoking relevant?
push.expect: Yes; smoking cessation is specifically recommended.

curveballs.prompt: Her thyroid function tests come back normal on treatment.
curveballs.safeAnswer: That does not exclude thyroid eye disease or reduce the urgency of the pupil and vision findings.

curveballs.prompt: She asks if her eyes will go back to normal once her thyroid is sorted.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not necessarily; eye disease can persist despite controlled thyroid function, and specialist follow-up is needed.

curveballs.prompt: She asks whether she needs eye surgery now.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not necessarily; surgical treatment is timed according to disease activity, and the urgent step now is specialist assessment of the sight-threatening features.
